title: ADT Explorer
description: Compare seven ADTs and their implementations.
objective: Choose an ADT by the operations and behavior a problem needs.
question: Which ADT serves items in arrival order?
explanation: A queue is first in, first out. Its behavior does not depend on the storage representation.
challenge: In Compare mode, run the same workload on two implementations. Explain which operations cause the cost difference.

title: Problem Types & Paradigms
description: Connect problem formulations with qualified algorithm examples.
objective: Separate what a problem asks from the strategy used to solve it.
question: Can a greedy algorithm be exact?
choices: Yes, when its choices can be justified
explanation: Huffman coding and Dijkstra on nonnegative weights are examples of exact greedy methods.
challenge: For the same packing constraints, write one decision question, one counting question, and one optimization question.

title: Hash Table Collision & Load Factor Lab
description: Trace probes, chaining, search, deletion, and rehashing.
objective: Explain collision handling and why a deleted probing slot cannot always become empty.
question: With capacity 7, where does key 16 start?
explanation: 16 % 7 = 2. A collision changes where probing eventually places it, not its home bucket.
challenge: Use 2, 9, 16 with linear probing. Remove 9, then search for 16. Explain the tombstone.

title: Binary Heap: Tree & Array
description: Explore a heap implementation of the Priority Queue ADT.
objective: Relate insert/remove-priority behavior to heap order.
question: Must the array representing a min-heap be fully sorted?
explanation: Heap order constrains each parent against its children, not arbitrary pairs of elements.
challenge: Generate a heap. Predict the next root before removing the current root. Then try Heapify & Heapsort.

title: BST & Tree Traversals
description: Compare search-tree shapes, operations, and traversal orders.
objective: Explain how ordering and tree height affect search.
question: What is the edge-count height of a single-node tree?
explanation: A leaf has zero edges on its longest downward path. An empty tree has height −1.
challenge: Compare a skewed and balanced tree with the same keys. Which search visits the most nodes? Try all three deletion presets.

title: AVL Rotation Lab
description: Predict balance repairs and preserve inorder order.
objective: Choose a rotation from the lowest imbalance and track the transferred middle subtree.
question: What does an AVL rotation preserve?
explanation: A rotation changes shape while preserving the BST ordering and inorder sequence.
challenge: Try LR and RL, then deletion. Before each rotation, identify the subtree that moves between the two nodes.

title: BFS & DFS Graph Explorer
description: Follow queues, recursive calls, discovery, and completion.
objective: Distinguish the traversal frontier from the traversal tree.
question: Which gives shortest edge-count distances in an unweighted graph?
explanation: BFS discovers vertices in increasing edge distance. DFS depth is generally different.
challenge: Use the disconnected preset. Predict how continuing across components changes the forest, then switch BFS to DFS on the same graph.

title: Graph Representation Lab
description: Compare a matrix and adjacency lists on the same graph.
objective: Choose a representation using operation and storage costs.
question: Which representation checks a known edge in constant time?
explanation: A matrix directly indexes the cell for the two endpoints. A sequential list may inspect several neighbors.
challenge: Choose an isolated vertex, then a dense graph. Compare absent-edge lookup and neighbor enumeration.

title: Dijkstra’s Shortest Paths
description: Inspect priority-queue selection and relaxation.
objective: Explain why the smallest tentative distance is settled next.
question: What edge-weight condition does this Dijkstra lesson require?
explanation: Nonnegative weights justify settling the smallest tentative distance permanently.
challenge: Try the disconnected and tied-route examples. Explain why two equal shortest routes need not produce the same predecessor tree.

title: Card Sort Visualizer
description: Trace four sorts, their invariants, and equal-key order.
objective: Explain a sorting step using its invariant and stability guarantee.
question: Does preserving equal-key order on one run prove an algorithm stable?
explanation: Stability is a guarantee for every valid input. An unstable algorithm can preserve order on some runs.
challenge: Use Many Duplicates. Find a selection-sort swap that reverses equal keys, then compare insertion and merge sort.

title: Card Sorting Workbench
description: Perform sorting passes manually and undo moves.
objective: Justify a manual move using a sorting rule.
question: After one full selection-sort pass, what is guaranteed?
explanation: The scan selects the minimum remaining item and moves it into the first unsorted position.
challenge: Perform one insertion-sort pass without disturbing the earlier sorted prefix. Use Undo to compare a different move sequence.

title: Asymptotic Bounds Lab
description: Explore constants, thresholds, and finite counterexamples.
objective: Distinguish a chosen witness from existence of an asymptotic bound.
question: Can a finite plot alone prove an asymptotic bound for all larger n?
explanation: A finite counterexample can refute chosen constants. A passing finite sample does not quantify over every larger input.
challenge: For f(n)=3n+8 and g(n)=n, find constants that fail, then constants and a threshold that work. Explain why Θ(n) stays true.

title: Divide & Conquer Recurrence Tree
description: Predict recursive levels and add their exact costs.
objective: Connect a recurrence, per-level work, and asymptotic growth.
question: In T(n)=2T(n/2)+n, what is the total work at each internal level?
explanation: At depth d there are 2^d subproblems, each with n/2^d work, so the product is n.
challenge: Predict node count, subproblem size, and level work before each Step. Then compare root-heavy and leaf-heavy examples.

title: Huffman Coding
description: Build prefix codes, encode, and decode.
objective: Relate greedy minimum-weight merges to weighted code length.
question: When weights tie, must every valid Huffman construction use identical bit strings?
explanation: Tie choices can change codewords while preserving the optimal weighted path length.
challenge: Use tied weights. Compare the encoded payload to fixed-length coding, then decode the stream. Explain codebook overhead.

title: Bin Packing
description: Compare packing heuristics on the same custom sequence.
objective: Separate heuristic outcomes, lower bounds, and known optima.
question: Is ceil(total item size) always an attainable bin count?
explanation: Items cannot be split. For 0.6, 0.6, 0.6 the volume bound is 2, but three bins are required.
challenge: Enter 0.6, 0.6, 0.6. Compare every rule and the exact small-instance result. Explain the gap above the volume bound.

title: Maximum Subarray Comparison Lab
description: Compare brute force, divide/conquer, and Kadane.
objective: Explain Kadane’s state and reconstruct a nonempty maximum interval.
question: For −8, −3, −6, what is the nonempty maximum-subarray sum?
explanation: The answer must contain an element; an empty interval with sum 0 is excluded.
challenge: Try tied solutions and all-negative inputs. Explain the tie rule and why divide/conquer must examine a crossing interval.

title: Recursion Call Stack
description: Trace calls, pending work, returns, and a call tree.
objective: Distinguish active calls from the complete call tree.
question: After a recursive call returns, where does execution resume?
choices: At the start of the program
In every previous call at once
explanation: The caller resumes with the returned value; only active calls remain on the stack.
challenge: Compare linear search, binary search, and Fibonacci. Point to the expression waiting for a return in each active caller.

title: List ADT Sequence Puzzles
description: Transform sequences with remove and insert operations.
objective: Plan a sequence transformation using only List ADT operations.
question: After removing index 1 from [10,20,30], what remains?
explanation: The List ADT is an ordered sequence. Removing index 1 removes the second element and changes subsequent positions.
challenge: Solve rotation and reversal puzzles. Explain each operation by its sequence effect, without relying on a storage implementation.

title: N-Queens Backtracking
description: Try candidates, prune conflicts, and undo placements.
objective: Explain how a partial assignment prunes a search subtree.
question: Why reject a partial queen placement with a diagonal conflict?
explanation: Extending a conflicting partial assignment cannot make the existing pair safe.
challenge: Find a 4-queen solution, then enumerate all solutions. Try the unsatisfiable 3×3 board and explain why the search must backtrack.

title: LCS & Traceback
description: Compare recursion, memoization, tabulation, and reconstruction.
objective: Build a prefix DP state and trace back one longest common subsequence.
question: Does a common subsequence have to occupy consecutive positions?
explanation: A subsequence preserves order but may skip positions; a substring must be contiguous.
challenge: Compare all three solution methods on AGCAT and GAC. Predict a DP cell, then explain a traceback tie.

title: Matrix-Chain Multiplication
description: Compare interval splits and reconstruct parentheses.
objective: Minimize scalar work without changing the matrix order.
question: What may change in matrix-chain optimization?
explanation: Matrix multiplication is associative, but the dimensions make different groupings have different scalar costs.
challenge: Try dimensions 10,100,5,50. Compute both parenthesizations before playing, then inspect the selected split tree.

title: Amortized Array Growth
description: Compare doubling and fixed increments over repeated appends.
objective: Separate one expensive operation from a sequence’s amortized cost.
question: Does O(1) amortized append mean every append has constant actual cost?
explanation: A resize can copy all current elements; the total over a sequence can still be linear.
challenge: Compare 20 appends under both policies. Identify every cost spike, then explain why doubling gives a linear total.

title: Heapify & Heapsort
description: Build a heap bottom-up and grow a sorted suffix.
objective: Explain bottom-up heapify and repeated root removal.
question: Which heap order produces ascending in-place heapsort here?
explanation: The maximum root moves to the rightmost unsorted position, growing the sorted suffix from right to left.
challenge: Compare heapify with repeated insertion on sorted and reversed arrays. Distinguish measured comparisons from worst-case growth.

title: Calculator Lexer
description: Trace source characters into typed tokens.
objective: Distinguish source characters, lexemes, token types, and lexical errors.
question: Is a valid token stream necessarily a valid expression?
explanation: For example, x + * y contains valid tokens but violates the expression grammar.
challenge: Try x1 + 12, then _x and 12a. Identify whether each failure is lexical or syntactic. Open the same input in the grammar lesson.

title: Grammar, Parse Tree & AST
description: Compare derivations, precedence, parse trees, and ASTs.
objective: Explain how grammar structure gives an expression meaning.
question: Which tree normally omits grammar scaffolding and grouping parentheses?
explanation: The AST retains the operators and operands needed to represent the expression structure.
challenge: Compare x+y*z, (x+y)*z, and x-y-z. Switch leftmost/rightmost derivations and explain why they can produce the same tree.
